title: The Failed Stove Workshop Five Mondragón Workers Bought in 1955
dek: Refused a share in the town's biggest firm, five young Basque workers bought a bankrupt workshop and began the first Mondragón cooperative.

story.founder: José María Arizmendiarrieta, Luis Usatorre, Jesús Larrañaga, Alfonso Gorroñogoitia, José María Ormaechea, Javier Ortubay
story.event: Buying a bankrupt stove workshop in Vitoria and moving it to Mondragón as the first cooperative
story.summary: In 1955 five young workers at Unión Cerrajera in Mondragón, former pupils of the priest José María Arizmendiarrieta's technical school, bought a bankrupt heater and stove workshop in Vitoria and began making paraffin cookers. They named it Ulgor after their surnames, moved it to Mondragón in 1956, where Arizmendiarrieta blessed the foundation stone on 14 April, and only settled its cooperative bylaws in 1958 or 1959. Ulgor became Fagor Electrodomésticos and the seed of the Mondragón cooperatives.
paragraphs: On 14 April 1956, on a plot called Laxarte at the edge of Mondragón, the priest José María Arizmendiarrieta blessed the foundation stone of a factory whose legal form was still unsettled. He had walked out to the site with José María Ormaechea, one of the five young men whose company it was, and Ormaechea measured out the ground, bought at 45 pesetas a square metre. About a fortnight later, work began on a two-storey concrete plant of 750 square metres.

Arizmendiarrieta had arrived in the Basque town in 1941, newly ordained, in a place still worn down by the civil war. Its dominant employer, Unión Cerrajera, ran an apprentice school that took only 12 boys a year, all sons of its own staff, and it kept that rule when he asked for a change. In 1943 he opened his own school instead, with 21 pupils. Eleven of its early students went on to study industrial engineering in Zaragoza; the first qualified in 1952.

Several of them were then working at the Cerrajera. According to witness testimony gathered by the Arizmendiarrieta Foundation, the priest had asked the firm's owners to let employees share in its ownership and got nowhere. He then urged a few young men to start their own company, with whatever capital they could put in themselves and their own work, on equal terms. In 1955 five of them, Luis Usatorre, Jesús Larrañaga, Alfonso Gorroñogoitia, Ormaechea and Javier Ortubay, bought a small bankrupt workshop in Vitoria that had made heaters and stoves, and began producing paraffin cookers. They called it Ulgor, from their surnames. They had no ready model: one history records several rejections and rewritten statutes before they saw that cooperative law fitted what they wanted.

In 1956 the workshop moved to Mondragón. Its first bylaws as Talleres Ulgor were approved only in May 1959, by the Mondragon group's own account; a reference history dates its conversion to a cooperative to 1958. In 1959 Ulgor and three other cooperatives also founded a savings bank, Caja Laboral Popular, at a time when, two Basque academics write, Ulgor had not yet solved its technical, sales or even legal problems. By 1970 one history counts 41 cooperatives in the region. Ulgor itself became Fagor Electrodomésticos.

quote.text: It remains then for thee to understand among what kind of workmen thou placest thyself; for he who rules all things will certainly make a right use of thee
quote.source_title: Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #15877
quote.connection: Marcus assumes that everyone ends up working at something; what is left to each person is the choice of which kind of workman to be. The five were already useful at the Cerrajera. In 1955 they chose to place themselves among a different kind of workmen.

reflection: This beginning was far from tidy: a refusal from the town's biggest employer, a priest's encouragement, a failed workshop in another town and the founders' own money. The legal form that made them a cooperative took years and several rejected drafts to find. They made cookers in the meantime and worked out the shape of the company as they went.

You do not need every structure settled before you begin something that matters. What the five did settle early was whose work it was; the name carried all their surnames. Knowing that plainly, about your own work and the people in it, can carry you a long way while the paperwork lags behind.
invitation: Ask one colleague you work closely with which part of your shared work feels most like theirs, and listen to the answer without trying to improve it.

cross_checks.claim: In 1955 five young men bought a small bankrupt workshop in Vitoria that made stoves and heaters, and moved it to Mondragón in 1956
The founders were Unión Cerrajera workers and former students of Arizmendiarrieta's school
Arizmendiarrieta blessed Ulgor's foundation stone on 14 April 1956
Arizmendiarrieta opened his technical school in 1943
The name Ulgor was formed from the five founders' surnames
Ulgor's cooperative form came after the founding, in 1958 or with bylaws approved in May 1959
Ulgor and other cooperatives founded Caja Laboral Popular in 1959

research_notes: Founding year: sources split between 1955 (the Vitoria purchase, per Altuna and Urteaga and the Gale encyclopedia) and 1956 (the move to Mondragón and the foundation stone, per the Mondragon Corporation, Fagor and Mondragon Unibertsitatea). The story dates the purchase to 1955 and the stone to 14 April 1956. Cooperative status: the Gale entry says the firm was converted to a cooperative in 1958; the Mondragon Corporation says the first bylaws of Talleres Ulgor were approved in May 1959; both are given and attributed. Product: Altuna and Urteaga say paraffin cookers (cocinas de petróleo), Elio says paraffin heaters and cookers, Gale says the Vitoria firm had made heaters and stoves; the story uses Gale's wording for the workshop and 'paraffin cookers' for Ulgor's first output. Omitted as weakly sourced: a co-operative presentation's claim that the five raised £60,000 in loans from 100 local people and that the stove was made under licence (George Benello's essay instead calls it a copied kerosene stove), and Benello's figure of 24 initial members. The capital is therefore described only as what the founders could put in themselves, from the Arizmendiarrieta Foundation's witness testimony; funding is set to bootstrapped because no outside investor was involved. The refusal by the Cerrajera's owners rests on that testimony and is attributed to it. Spelling: the Basque form Ormaetxea and the Spanish Ormaechea both appear; the story uses Ormaechea, as the Mondragon Corporation does. The Gale entry spells the priest 'Arizmendiarreta'. The Mondragon Unibertsitatea page calls the 1952 graduates 'industrial surveyors' (peritos industriales); the story says they qualified in industrial engineering, following Gale's 'industrial technical engineering'. Several sources are Spanish-language PDFs; claims were read from their full text. The 41 cooperatives by 1970 is Elio's count. The quote comes from Marcus Aurelius's reflection that all people co-operate in the work of the universe in different fashions; it is applied here by analogy.
